title: Rituals are leaky boats (1.2)
hook: the Mundaka praises the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats, and both statements sit side by side in the same chapter
tomorrow: go to a teacher, fuel in hand

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spider and the web, and your line, as the spider. Did a web or a stubborn plant remind you of the three pictures? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of week fifty-nine.

A rowboat can be a perfectly good boat. It'll take you around the lake, out to the dock, across to the picnic spot. Now try to cross an ocean in it. Nothing about the boat has changed. What changed is where you're trying to go. The second section of the Mundaka does something bold with that idea. It's talking about the great fire rites of the Vedas, the ones priests spent lifetimes learning. First, it honors them. Then it calls them boats. And then it tells you what kind of boats.
screen: `A GOOD ROWBOAT.` → `NOW CROSS AN OCEAN IN IT.` → `THE RITES ARE BOATS.`

segments.voice: The section opens with a clear yes. This is the truth, it says: the rites the sages saw in the sacred verses are spread out in many ways. Practice them faithfully. This is your path to the world of good deeds. Then it describes the fire offering in loving detail, the seven flickering tongues of flame, each with a name: the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, the deep red, the smoky, the sparkling, the one of every shape. And then the turn. Plava hy ete adridha yajnarupah. Unsteady, indeed, are these boats, the eighteen forms of sacrifice. Fools who praise them as the highest good go again and again to old age and death. Thinking themselves wise, the text says, they wander around like the blind led by the blind. They enjoy the heaven their good works earned, and then, when it runs out, they come back down. So which is it? Are the rites true or leaky? The Mundaka says both, on purpose. The rites really do what they promise. They earn a good world. But a good world is still a world that ends. They're boats for the lake, not the ocean. And then the line that explains the whole section: the uncreated is not won by what is made. Nasty akritah kritena. Nothing you build, however holy, can build your way to the unbuilt. Different schools weighed this differently. The Mimamsa tradition held ritual itself as the heart of the Veda. Vedanta teachers read this passage as the turn toward knowledge. Many Hindus today keep the rites and the inner search together.
screen: `FIRST: THE RITES ARE TRUE.` · `SEVEN TONGUES OF FLAME.` · `THEN: UNSTEADY BOATS.` · `THE UNMADE ISN'T WON BY THE MADE.` · then, large: `PLAVA HY ETE ADRIDHA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the boat. Think of one thing you do faithfully, a habit, a ritual, a routine that's good for you. Honor it for a breath: it works, it carries you. Then ask gently: where is it carrying me? And is there somewhere it can't go? Don't answer quickly. Then let the question go and just sit, not doing anything at all for a moment. Nothing made, nothing earned. The bell holds the time.
Rituals are leaky boats. The Mundaka honors the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats: they earn good worlds, but the uncreated isn't won by what's made.

Your line: the boat leaks. Today, keep doing your good routines, and once, ask where you're rowing. And that's week fifty-nine: breath leaves, a shadow, awake in sleep, sixteen parts, two knowledges, the spider, and the leaky boats. Day four hundred thirteen.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-NINE: BREATH · SHADOW · SLEEP · SIXTEEN PARTS · TWO KNOWLEDGES · THE SPIDER · THE BOATS`

howItsDone: Many Hindus keep daily and seasonal rites, from lighting a lamp to fire offerings (homa), while also studying texts like the Mundaka that point beyond ritual; teachers often explain this passage as a lesson about motive, not a call to stop.

myth: the Mundaka says Vedic rites are false and useless
it calls them true, then says they're unsteady boats for crossing beyond death.
the text names seven tongues of the sacred fire
the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, and four more.
the heaven earned by rites lasts forever, in this text
when the merit runs out, they come back down.

fork.setup: you've done the fire rites faithfully all your life. the Mundaka says they're true. what does it say they can't do?
options: they can't earn any good world.
they can't carry you across to the uncreated.
they can't be done by householders.
fork.reveal: they earn a good world that ends. the unmade is not won by what is made: nasty akritah kritena.

original.note: Sanskrit plava, a boat or float: 'unsteady boats are these forms of sacrifice', Mundaka 1.2.7.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Upanishads reject ritual.
what it means: the Mundaka calls the rites true and good, and also unsteady boats that can't cross to the uncreated.
what a scholar hears: plavā hy ete adṛḍhā yajñarūpā aṣṭādaśa (1.2.7); commentators count the eighteen as sixteen priests plus the sacrificer and his wife.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.1–1.2.12 (the rites are true; seven tongues; blind led by the blind; the uncreated)

notes: Seven tongues (1.2.4): Kali, Karali, Manojava, Sulohita, Sudhumravarna, Sphulingini, Vishvaruci, glossed loosely. Confirm.
Eighteen = 16 priests + yajamana + patni is Shankara's count; confirm.
Mimamsa characterization ('held ritual itself as the heart of the Veda') is brief; confirm fairness.
